relationship: Campaign narrative parallel: Joab besieges Ammon while David stays home
rationale: Both place Joab's campaign against Ammon at the return of the campaigning year and leave David in Jerusalem. Chronicles also compresses the striking and razing of Rabba into this notice; Samuel names the besieged city Rabbah.

relationship: Campaign development: Joab's siege and David's arrival
rationale: Chronicles compresses Joab's siege and destruction of Rabba; Samuel expands the capture at Rabbah through Joab's message and David's arrival. The accounts distribute the actions differently and are not made into identical descriptions.

relationship: Spoil narrative parallel: the royal crown
rationale: Both describe a royal crown weighing a talent of gold, a precious stone, its placement on David's head, and abundant spoil. Chronicles names Molchol and Samuel Melchol; each form is retained.

relationship: Conquest aftermath parallel with distinct treatment wording
rationale: Both describe David bringing out the inhabitants, treatment involving saws and iron implements, further action against Ammon, and return to Jerusalem. Chronicles explicitly says he sawed them apart with saws and iron adzes; Samuel describes the saw, threshing implements, and brickworks.

relationship: Battle-notice comparison with distinct names and sites
rationale: Both record renewed war with the foreigners and the defeat of a giant descendant. Chronicles names Sobochai the Ousathi, Saphou, and Gazer; Samuel names Sebocha the Astatothite, Seph, and Gath. The comparison preserves these differences without resolving personal or place identities.

relationship: Battle-notice comparison with distinct victim and patronymic
rationale: Both notices record a warrior striking an opponent in war with the foreigners and include the distinctive comparison of a spear shaft to a weaver's beam. Chronicles has Ellanan son of Jair strike Leemi, brother of Goliath; Samuel has Elhanan son of Ariorgim strike Goliath. Neither the victim nor the patronymic is harmonized.

relationship: Giant-battle parallel: twenty-four digits
rationale: Both describe a giant in renewed war with twenty-four digits. Chronicles says six and six and leaves the man unnamed at Geth; Samuel calls him Madon at Gath and explicitly describes six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot. Each account's wording and descent description remain distinct.

relationship: Battle parallel: Israel's taunter struck by David's nephew
rationale: Both record the giant taunting Israel and being struck by Jonathan, whose father is identified as David's brother. The father is Samaa in Chronicles and Shimei in Samuel; the stated kinship is compared without independently resolving those name forms.

relationship: Same-chapter grammatical connection: the giant who reproached Israel
rationale: The pronoun he continues the preceding description of the exceptionally large man with twenty-four digits. The target supplies the subject of the taunt and of Jonathan's subsequent victory.

relationship: Battle-cycle summary parallel: four giant descendants fall
rationale: Both summaries count four giant descendants associated with Rapha and state that they fell by David's hand and his servants' hands. Chronicles says Geth and Samuel Gath, retaining each summary's place wording.

relationship: Census narrative parallel with different stated instigator
rationale: Both introduce David's numbering of Israel through an incitement. Chronicles explicitly names the devil; Samuel begins with the Lord's anger and says He incited David. The link records the shared census setting while preserving the difference in agency.

relationship: Census command parallel: Joab must report the people's number
rationale: Both have the king send Joab through Israel to learn the people's number. Chronicles addresses Joab and the force's rulers and orders Bersabee to Dan; Samuel addresses Joab the commander and gives Dan to Beersheba.

relationship: Census objection parallel: Joab asks why the king desires it
rationale: Joab wishes for a hundredfold increase within the king's sight and questions the census in both passages. Chronicles additionally calls the people the king's servants and warns that the demand may become sin for Israel.

relationship: Census itinerary parallel: royal insistence and return to Jerusalem
rationale: Both say the king's word prevailed over Joab and describe travel through the land followed by return to Jerusalem. Samuel gives the intervening itinerary and nine months and twenty days; Chronicles summarizes the journey.

relationship: Census totals comparison with unreconciled numbers
rationale: Both make Joab report the armed population to the king. Chronicles gives Israel 1,100,000 and Judah 480,000; Samuel gives Israel 800,000 and Judah 500,000. The comparison retains each account's totals rather than combining them.

relationship: Same-chapter census qualification: excluded tribes
rationale: The statement that Levi and Benjamin were not numbered qualifies Joab's preceding census journey and reported totals. The repeated overpowering of Joab ties the omission to the narrative's royal command without supplying an unstated alternative count.

relationship: Same-chapter narrative judgment: the census Joab questioned
rationale: The matter judged evil is the numbering introduced by the incitement and David's order. Joab's warning that it could become sin for Israel gives the explicit preceding objection to the action God now judges.

relationship: Confession parallel: David admits foolishness after the census
rationale: David confesses great sin, asks removal of his servant's wickedness or lawlessness, and acknowledges extreme folly in both accounts. Samuel explicitly places the confession after David's heart struck him following the count.

relationship: Prophetic-message parallel: the Lord addresses David's seer
rationale: Both introduce the Lord's word to Gad as David's seer. Samuel also calls Gad a prophet and places the message in the morning.

relationship: Judgment-choice parallel: three alternatives offered to David
rationale: Both divine messages send Gad to David with three things laid against him and require him to select one. The following verses supply the contents of the three alternatives.

relationship: Same-chapter commission and delivery: Gad conveys the choice
rationale: Gad's arrival and opening command to choose enact the preceding divine commission to speak to David. The target identifies the sender and explains the authority of the otherwise incomplete introductory speech.

relationship: Prophetic-delivery parallel: Gad presents the alternatives
rationale: Chronicles introduces Gad's words with choose for yourself and continues the alternatives in the next unit; Samuel includes the same choosing command within the complete message of famine, flight, or death.

relationship: Judgment alternatives parallel: famine, flight, or death
rationale: Both offer three years of famine, three months before enemies, or three days of death and ask what reply Gad should bring. Chronicles additionally describes the enemies' sword and the Lord's sword and destroying angel throughout Israel's inheritance.

relationship: Response parallel: falling into the Lord's compassionate hand
rationale: David tells Gad in both texts that he is pressed on every side and prefers the Lord's hand because of His many compassions, refusing human hands. Samuel also explicitly says David chose death for himself.

relationship: Judgment result parallel: seventy thousand deaths
rationale: Both attribute the death sent on Israel to the Lord and count seventy thousand dead. Samuel adds the wheat-harvest setting, the time span, and Dan-to-Beersheba extent absent from this shorter Chronicles unit.

relationship: Mercy narrative parallel: the angel halted at Orna's floor
rationale: Both depict the angel threatening Jerusalem, the Lord relenting and ordering the hand withdrawn, and the angel at the threshing floor of Orna the Jebusite. These details connect the cessation of destruction to the later altar location.

relationship: Vision and intercession connection: David sees the destroying angel
rationale: Chronicles describes David seeing the angel with drawn sword over Jerusalem and falling down with the sackcloth-clad elders. Samuel says David saw the angel striking the people before interceding; it does not supply Chronicles' sword position or the elders.

relationship: Intercession parallel: David accepts guilt and pleads for the sheep
rationale: Both speeches distinguish David's own wrongdoing from the people called sheep and ask that the hand fall on him and his father's house. Chronicles explicitly recalls his census order and asks that the people escape destruction.

relationship: Altar-command parallel: Gad directs David to Orna's floor
rationale: Both direct David through Gad to establish an altar on Orna the Jebusite's threshing floor. Chronicles additionally identifies the Lord's angel as the one who instructed Gad.

relationship: Obedience parallel: David goes up according to Gad's word
rationale: Both state that David ascended according to Gad's word and explicitly connect that instruction with the Lord's authority.

relationship: Arrival scene parallel with bounded description of Orna's household
rationale: Both depict Orna seeing the approaching king at the threshing floor. Chronicles adds wheat threshing and four sons described as methachabin; Samuel describes the king's servants and Orna's bow. The untranslated term is not assigned a meaning.

relationship: Royal reception parallel: Orna bows face to the ground
rationale: Both have Orna come out to bow before the king with his face to the ground. Chronicles first says David came to Ornan and then names the bowing man Orna, preserving both forms within the source unit.

relationship: Purchase request parallel: an altar to stop the plague
rationale: David requests the threshing floor for an altar in both texts so that the devastation may stop among the people. Chronicles explicitly offers its worth in silver; Samuel gives the exchange as David's answer to Orna's question.

relationship: Gift offer parallel: animals and wooden equipment for sacrifice
rationale: Both have Orna offer the animals for the burnt offering, equipment for fuel, and everything needed to the king. Chronicles lists calves, plow, wagons, and grain; Samuel lists oxen, wheels, and oxen's equipment and adds a blessing.

relationship: Costly-offering parallel: David refuses a free gift
rationale: Both record David refusing to take Orna's goods without payment and refusing a whole burnt offering that costs him nothing. Samuel then reports a purchase price; Chronicles states its own amount in the next unit.

relationship: Purchase-price comparison with distinct sums and metals
rationale: Both record David paying Orna in the altar-site transaction. Chronicles says six hundred shekels of gold by weight at his site; Samuel says fifty shekels of silver for the threshing floor and oxen. The different sums, metals, and described objects remain distinct.

relationship: Altar-response parallel with additional heavenly fire in Chronicles
rationale: Both describe David building the altar and presenting whole burnt offerings with a further offering, followed by divine response. Chronicles names a deliverance offering and consuming fire from heaven; Samuel names peace offerings and the restraint of devastation.

relationship: Same-chapter narrative resolution: the drawn sword is sheathed
rationale: The angel's sheathing of the sword completes the earlier order to relax his hand and the vision of that sword stretched over Jerusalem. The link traces the stated weapon and cessation of the threat.

relationship: Same-chapter explanation: divine answer establishes David's sacrifice site
rationale: The later statement that David sacrificed at Orna's floor because the Lord answered him refers back to the altar, offerings, and heavenly fire just narrated there.

relationship: Sanctuary-location continuity: the tent and burnt-offering altar at Gabaon
rationale: Both place the Lord's tent and burnt-offering worship at Bama in Gabaon. The earlier passage names Sadok and the priests and their continual offerings; the source explains where the Mosaic tent and altar still stood during David's sacrifice elsewhere.

relationship: Same-chapter motive: withdrawal from the angel's sword
rationale: David's inability to seek God at the tent is explicitly related to the angel's sword. The earlier vision supplies the drawn sword over Jerusalem that explains this stated obstacle.

relationship: Same-chapter grammatical connection: the sanctuary David could not approach
rationale: The pronoun it refers back to the Lord's tent and burnt-offering altar at Bama in Gabaon. Reading the units together distinguishes that sanctuary from the altar David has just built at Orna's floor.

relationship: Narrative transition: the answered altar becomes the designated site
rationale: David's declaration about the Lord's house and Israel's burnt-offering altar follows the altar built at Orna's floor, the divine answer by fire, and David's continued sacrifice there. The target supplies the immediate site-setting for this declaration.

relationship: Temple preparation continuity: stoneworkers and prepared materials
rationale: David appoints quarrymen to dress stones for God's house; Solomon's building preparations include stonecutters, overseers, and prepared stones and timber. Kings does not identify those workers as David's resident foreigners, so the comparison concerns the work rather than personal identity.

relationship: Preparation reprise: David supplies iron and bronze for God's house
rationale: Both describe David preparing iron and bronze for the temple. The source specifies doorway nails and hinges and unweighed bronze; the later address includes those metals among the fuller collection of building materials.

relationship: Supply connection with distinct building projects: Tyrian cedar for David
rationale: Both record cedar reaching David from the Tyrian sphere. The source places Sidonian and Tyrian cedar in temple preparation; the earlier account names Chiram of Tyre supplying David's own house. The projects remain distinct.

relationship: Temple-material continuity: Sidonian skill and cedar supply
rationale: David receives abundant cedar from Sidonians and Tyrians; Solomon requests timber with Sidonian expertise, and Hiram promises and supplies cedar. The link follows the stated material and supplier tradition without assigning David's timber to a particular later shipment.

relationship: Preparation rationale reprise: Solomon's youth and the great divine house
rationale: Both addresses call Solomon young or tender and emphasize the greatness of the building for God. David responds in each by describing extensive preparation, while the source also specifies preparation before his death.

relationship: Commission reprise: Solomon is to build the Lord's sanctuary
rationale: David commands Solomon to build God's house; the later assembly speech attributes that choice to God, names Solomon, and exhorts him to be strong and act in building the sanctuary.

relationship: Recalled intention: David desired to build the house for the divine name
rationale: David tells Solomon that building the house came upon his soul; Solomon later recalls the same intention in David's heart and the Lord's response assigning construction to his son.

relationship: Prohibition reprise: David's warfare and bloodshed
rationale: Both reports of God's speech prohibit David from building the house because he was a warrior who had shed blood. The source stresses much blood and great wars before God.

relationship: Related explanation with different emphasis: David could not build amid wars
rationale: David reports the divine prohibition because of bloodshed and wars; Solomon tells Hiram his father could not build because of surrounding wars. The speeches connect the delayed building to warfare without equating every stated reason.

relationship: Promise and later testimony: rest enables Solomon's building
rationale: David reports that Solomon will receive rest from enemies and peace in Israel; Solomon later tells Hiram the Lord has given him rest on every side and announces his intention to build the promised house.

relationship: Davidic promise recalled: the son builds and receives an enduring throne
rationale: Both divine promises join David's successor's building of God's house with father-son language and an enduring throne. The source addresses the promise in the speech identifying Solomon, while the earlier oracle speaks of David's coming offspring.

relationship: Promise reprise with stated condition: Solomon's house and kingdom
rationale: Both reports name the son as God's son, God as his Father, and his kingdom as established. The later speech explicitly names Solomon and adds the condition of strength in observing God's commandments and judgments.

relationship: Encouragement reprise: divine presence through the building work
rationale: David assures Solomon of the Lord's presence and success in building the house; the later encouragement promises God's presence until the work of ministry in that house is finished.

relationship: Prayer and subsequent gift: understanding for Solomon's rule
rationale: David asks the Lord to give Solomon wisdom and understanding over Israel; Solomon later requests a discerning heart to judge God's people, and God grants a wise and discerning heart. The source also ties wisdom to observing the law.

relationship: Commissioning pattern: courage and obedience to Moses' instruction
rationale: David joins strength, courage, freedom from fear, and success to keeping the ordinances commanded through Moses. Joshua's commission similarly joins courage and divine presence with careful obedience to Moses' law and prosperity.

relationship: Exhortation reprise: be strong, act, and do not fear
rationale: Both exhortations from David to Solomon urge courage and strength and prohibit fear in the building commission. The source grounds success in keeping Mosaic judgments; the later speech emphasizes God's continuing presence through the work.

relationship: Material-preparation comparison with distinct inventories
rationale: Both record David's prepared gold, silver, bronze, iron, timber, and stones for God's house. The source gives 100,000 talents of gold and 1,000,000 of silver; the later speech distinguishes additional personal gold and silver from what was already prepared, so its amounts are not substituted for these.

relationship: Workforce continuity: skilled workers available to Solomon
rationale: David describes abundant artisans, stone builders, woodworkers, and skilled labor; the later assurance says eager and wise craftspeople are ready with the priests, Levites, rulers, and people for Solomon's work.

relationship: Same-chapter commissioning conclusion: materials and workers support action
rationale: The concluding charge to arise and act follows the specified stores of metals, timber, and stones and the available skilled workforce. The source's uncounted metals and divine-presence blessing turn those provisions into a practical building commission.

relationship: Support for Solomon: rulers ready for the temple commission
rationale: David commands Israel's rulers to support Solomon; the later speech assures Solomon that the rulers and all the people are ready for his words alongside the workers and service courses.

relationship: Divine-rest connection: enemies subdued before the building charge
rationale: David's appeal to rulers grounds their task in the Lord's presence and the land's subjection. The earlier oracle recounts God's presence with David, destruction and humbling of enemies, and a secure place for Israel.

relationship: Building purpose and later completion: a house with a place for the ark
rationale: David commands a sanctuary to receive the covenant ark and holy vessels; Solomon later says he built the house and made there a place for the ark containing the covenant. The target specifically confirms the ark's place, not every vessel mentioned in the command.

relationship: Commission reprise: wholehearted seeking and sanctuary construction
rationale: David calls for hearts and souls to seek God and for action in building the sanctuary. His later words to Solomon again join a whole heart and willing soul, seeking God, and the command to build the chosen sanctuary.

relationship: Succession connection: Solomon takes David's throne
rationale: The source reports David making Solomon king in his place; the later gathering makes Solomon king a second time and reports him seated on David's throne. The second-time wording is preserved rather than collapsing the notices into one ceremony.

relationship: Assembly connection: David gathers Israel's rulers
rationale: Both passages introduce an assembly convened by David for the closing organization of royal and temple affairs. The source includes priests and Levites; the later gathering enumerates Israel's rulers, officers, and warriors in detail.

relationship: Same-chapter census comparison: thirty and twenty as stated thresholds
rationale: The source numbers 38,000 Levites from thirty years upward; the later summary and David's last words set the ministry registration from twenty upward. Both thresholds are retained, with the later text itself associating the arrangement with settled worship and no further tent carrying.

relationship: Same-chapter numerical allocation: workers and officials from the Levite total
rationale: Of these refers to the 38,000 counted Levites in the target. The source allocates 24,000 to oversight of the house's works and 6,000 to scribal and judicial roles, identifying how these assignments belong to that census.

relationship: Same-chapter numerical allocation: gatekeepers and musicians complete the roster
rationale: The two groups of 4,000 follow the 24,000 supervisors and 6,000 scribes and judges. Together the stated allocations account for the target's total of 38,000 Levites, with the source distinguishing gatekeeping from instrumental praise.

relationship: Worship organization continuity: praise with instruments and gate duty
rationale: The source allocates Levites to instrumental praise and gatekeeping. The earlier arrangement likewise names people praising the Lord with instruments and places Idithon's sons at the gate, showing those stated functions before the later numerical allocation.

relationship: Levitical division comparison with retained name forms
rationale: Both organize Levi's descendants through three named sons. Chronicles gives Gedson, Kaath, and Merari; Numbers gives Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. The parallel structural role is compared without turning the differing forms into independently proven identities.

relationship: Same-chapter roster continuation: Edan and Semei expanded
rationale: The source's brief and according to Parosom, Edan, and Semei is followed by the lists headed Edan's sons and Semei's sons. The target expands the latter named headings; it does not define Parosom or replace the source's unusual wording.

relationship: Same-chapter named heading and descendants: Edan's three sons
rationale: The preceding heading names Edan; the source supplies Jiiel the ruler, Zethom, and Joel as his three sons. The connection explains the list's placement without assigning the names to a different genealogy.

relationship: Same-chapter roster connection with retained ancestry wording
rationale: The preceding units name Edan and Semei and give Edan's three sons. The source then lists Salomith, Jiiel, and Aidan as Semei's sons but calls them ancestral rulers of Edan; the connection preserves both statements rather than rewriting the family heading.

relationship: Same-chapter family-list explanation: four sons and their inspection
rationale: The source names Semei's four sons, Jeth, Ziza, Joas, and Beria. The next unit ranks the first two and explains why Joas and Beria formed one ancestral house for inspection, supplying the administrative significance of the list.

relationship: Same-chapter family-list antecedent: the ranked and combined sons
rationale: Jeth, Ziza, Joas, and Beria in this allocation are the four sons just listed under Semei. The target identifies the family group whose first and second places and combined inspection are being described.

relationship: Genealogical grouping repeated: Ambram, Issaar, Chebron, and Oziel
rationale: The source identifies these four as Kaath's sons; the later treasury section repeats the same four names as its heading. The link follows the exact named grouping without importing an unstated assignment for each individual.

relationship: Priestly appointment connection: Aaron and his sons set apart
rationale: Chronicles distinguishes Aaron and his sons for holy ministry, incense, and invoking the Lord's name. Exodus directly commands bringing Aaron and his sons from Israel to serve as priests, grounding the stated distinction in a priestly appointment.

relationship: Priestly responsibility connection: Aaron and his sons over sanctuary service
rationale: The source describes Aaron's enduring consecration with his sons for ministry before the Lord. Numbers appoints Aaron and his sons over the Tent, priesthood, altar, and inner sanctuary, giving specific responsibilities corresponding to that distinct service.

relationship: Same-chapter family distinction: Moses' sons remain in Levi
rationale: The source places Moses' sons within Levi after the account of Aaron's distinct consecration with his sons for priestly ministry. The preceding unit identifies Aaron and Moses as Ambram's sons and explains the distinction being made between the brothers' descendant groups.

relationship: Moses' sons comparison with retained names
rationale: Chronicles names Moses' sons Gersam and Eliezer; Exodus describes his two sons as Gershom and Eliezer and their return with his wife and father-in-law. The connection retains the different first-son name form while comparing the explicitly stated father and two-son family.

relationship: Genealogical and office connection: Soubael in Moses' line
rationale: The source names Soubael the ruler among Gersam's sons. The later treasury notice explicitly places Soubael in the descent of Gersam and Moses and assigns him leadership over the treasuries.

relationship: Same-chapter genealogy continuation: Eliezer's line expanded
rationale: The earlier unit names Eliezer as one of Moses' two sons. The source develops that line through Raabia, states Eliezer had no other sons, and contrasts Raabia's numerous descendants with the one-son generation.

relationship: Same-chapter genealogy continuation: Issaar's branch
rationale: Issaar is one of Kaath's four sons in the heading; the source supplies Salomoth as ruler among Issaar's sons. The connection locates this short branch notice within the named Kaath family.

relationship: Same-chapter genealogy continuation: Chebron's four sons
rationale: Chebron appears among Kaath's sons in the heading. The source expands his branch through Idoud, Amadia, Oziel, and Ikemias and states their order, without equating this line with differently headed lists elsewhere.

relationship: Same-chapter genealogy continuation: Oziel's branch
rationale: The heading lists Oziel among Kaath's four sons; the source gives Michas and Isia as Oziel's sons, ranking them first and second. The repeated family heading establishes the branch's place in the roster.

relationship: Same-chapter branch structure: Merari's descendants
rationale: David's division heading names Merari among Levi's sons. The source develops that branch through Mooli and Mousi and then Mooli's sons Eleazar and Kis, explaining the scope of the next family notices.

relationship: Same-chapter kinship explanation: Eleazar's daughters and Kis's sons
rationale: The preceding genealogy identifies Eleazar and Kis as Mooli's sons. That stated relationship explains why the sons of Kis who marry Eleazar's daughters are described here as their kinsmen.

relationship: Repeated genealogy: Mousi's three sons
rationale: Both passages name Mooli, Eder, and Jarimoth as Mousi's sons. The source counts three, while the later roster places the line within the Levites' ancestral houses.

relationship: Same-chapter ministry census explanation: twenty years and house service
rationale: The source summarizes registration by ancestral houses from twenty upward for the house's ministry. The later units repeat twenty as the threshold in David's last words and explain the placement of the Levites at Aaron's hand for that ministry.

relationship: Same-chapter explanation: settled worship ends transport duties
rationale: David's statement that God has given rest and dwells in Jerusalem leads directly to the statement that the Levites no longer carried the tent and its vessels. The target shows the practical consequence for the service arrangement being explained.

relationship: Levitical-duty contrast: tent carrying formerly assigned
rationale: Chronicles says the Levites were no longer carrying the tent and its vessels. Numbers explicitly assigns Gershon's division the carrying of tent curtains, coverings, and utensils under priestly direction, identifying a former transport duty now said to cease.

relationship: Levitical-duty contrast: Merari's former carrying charge
rationale: The source's cessation of tent carrying contrasts with the earlier assignment of tent structures, court fittings, pegs, cords, and utensils to Merari's division. The target concerns carrying responsibilities rather than an end to all Levitical service.

relationship: Same-chapter census contrast: David's last words use twenty
rationale: The source explicitly associates the age of twenty and upward with David's last words. The earlier census uses thirty and upward; retaining both notices records the text's different thresholds without replacing either.

relationship: Ministry continuity: Levites stationed to serve Aaron
rationale: Chronicles stations Levites at Aaron's hand for work in the Lord's house, courts, chambers, and purification. Numbers sets Levi before Aaron to minister to him and keep the Tent's charges and furnishings, providing the earlier institutional arrangement.

relationship: Bread-service connection: presentation bread and its ordinance
rationale: The source includes presentation bread and fine flour among the Levites' duties. Leviticus specifies twelve fine-flour loaves, their placement before the Lord, weekly renewal, and Aaron's sons' portion; it supplies the ordinance for this named bread service.

relationship: Grain-offering preparation connection: unleavened and pan foods
rationale: The source lists fine flour, unleavened flat cakes, and pan and mixed preparations. Leviticus prescribes fine-flour offerings baked as unleavened loaves or wafers and prepared on a griddle or hearth with oil, illuminating those specifically named kinds of preparation.

relationship: Daily worship connection: praise alongside recurring offerings
rationale: The source appoints morning and evening praise and thanksgiving. The earlier arrangement combines morning and evening burnt offerings with named men who praise the Lord and use instruments, placing the daily praise duty within the stated worship order.

relationship: Calendar-offering ordinance: sabbaths and new moons
rationale: Chronicles assigns service over the numbered offerings on sabbaths, new moons, and feasts. Numbers gives the particular sabbath and new-moon animals and accompanying offerings; it specifies two of the occasions named in the source without purporting to exhaust the feast schedule.

relationship: Sanctuary-charge continuity: Levites and Aaron's sons
rationale: Both coordinate the Levites' keeping of the Tent's charges with Aaron and his sons' priestly service. Numbers distinguishes the Levites' assistance from restricted altar and inner-sanctuary duties, while Chronicles summarizes the brothers' ministry in the house.

relationship: Priestly family list parallel with retained name forms
rationale: Both list Aaron's four sons as the priestly family: Chronicles has Nadab, Abioud, Eleazar, and Ithamar; Numbers has Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar and calls them anointed priests. The differing second name is retained.

relationship: Priestly appointment and roster connection: Aaron's sons
rationale: Chronicles introduces divisions through Aaron's four sons; Exodus commands Aaron and his named sons to serve as priests. The link compares the stated family and office while keeping Chronicles' Abioud and Exodus's Abihu as written.

relationship: Priestly succession parallel: death without sons and surviving priests
rationale: Both record the deaths of Nadab and the second named son, followed by Eleazar and Ithamar serving as priests. Chronicles names Abioud, says they died before their father, and reports no sons; Numbers names Abihu, supplies the strange-fire setting before the Lord, and reports no children.

relationship: Same-chapter division procedure: the two priestly branches
rationale: David, Sadok, and Achimelech organize ministry by ancestral houses. The following units specify the sixteen Eleazar houses and eight Ithamar houses, the lots, and the secretary's recording before the assembled leadership, explaining how the division was carried out.

relationship: Same-chapter priestly genealogy and allocation: sixteen and eight houses
rationale: The source allocates sixteen ancestral rulers to Eleazar's sons and eight to Ithamar's sons. The preceding units explain why these two surviving priestly branches, represented by Sadok and Achimelech, are the groups being divided.

relationship: Same-chapter procedure and result: twenty-four priestly lots
rationale: The source says the two priestly branches were divided by lot because both contained sacred rulers. The ensuing list gives the actual first through twenty-fourth lot outcomes, making the procedure concrete without assigning an unstated branch to each listed name.

relationship: Same-chapter official record: the division is witnessed and written
rationale: Samaias records the alternating ancestral houses before the king and assembled priestly leadership. The target supplies the division's organizers, unequal branch totals, and lot procedure that his record documents; the alternating wording is not used to erase the sixteen-to-eight totals.

relationship: Same-chapter lot-list scope: Jarib and Ideia
rationale: Jarib's first lot and Ideia's second are the opening outcomes of the priestly division by lots recorded by Samaias before the king and priestly leaders. The target supplies the procedure and witnessed setting for these two otherwise brief allocations.

relationship: Same-chapter lot-list scope: Charem and Seorim
rationale: The third lot for Charem and fourth for Seorim continue the recorded division of the priestly ancestral houses. The target establishes that these numbered placements were determined by lots and officially recorded, rather than describing unrelated personal deeds.

relationship: Same-chapter lot-list scope: Melchia and Miamin
rationale: Melchia's fifth place and Miamin's sixth belong to the priestly lots described and recorded in the target. The connection supplies the allocation procedure and assembly that govern the source's two names and ordinals.

relationship: Same-chapter lot-list scope: Kos and Abia
rationale: The seventh lot for Kos and eighth for Abia are two outcomes of the division by lots witnessed and recorded before the king and priests. This identifies their role within the list without equating Abia with a similarly named figure elsewhere.

relationship: Same-chapter lot-list scope: Jesus and Sechenia
rationale: Jesus receives the ninth lot and Sechenia the tenth within the priestly division. The target identifies the lot procedure and official record to which the two entries belong; no later person is identified merely from either name.

relationship: Same-chapter lot-list scope: Eliasib and Jakim
rationale: The eleventh and twelfth places assigned to Eliasib and Jakim continue the recorded priestly lots. The target explains the sacred-leadership setting and the secretary's record of the ancestral houses being allocated.

relationship: Same-chapter lot-list scope: Ochchopha and Isbaal
rationale: Ochchopha's thirteenth lot and Isbaal's fourteenth are entries in the procedure that divided the priestly houses by lots and recorded them before their leaders. The connection supplies this administrative role without supplying unrecorded ancestry for either name.

relationship: Same-chapter lot-list scope: Belga and Emmer
rationale: The fifteenth and sixteenth lots for Belga and Emmer continue the witnessed priestly allocation. The target establishes the governing lot procedure; the source's sixteenth position is not by itself treated as a boundary between Eleazar's and Ithamar's houses.

relationship: Same-chapter lot-list scope: Chezir and Aphesse
rationale: Chezir and Aphesse receive the seventeenth and eighteenth lots within the priestly ancestral-house division. The preceding explanation of lots and Samaias's recording gives these two entries their service-allocation context.

relationship: Same-chapter lot-list scope: Phetaia and Ezekiel
rationale: Phetaia's nineteenth and Ezekiel's twentieth lots belong to the officially recorded priestly division described in the target. The names are retained as roster entries without identifying them with other bearers of similar names.

relationship: Same-chapter lot-list scope: Jachin and Gamoul
rationale: The twenty-first and twenty-second lots for Jachin and Gamoul continue the division of priestly ancestral houses by lots. The target supplies the procedure and witnesses for their numbered positions.

relationship: Same-chapter lot-list scope: Dalaia and Maasai
